==> framework--bompa-annual-plan-cycle-types.md <==

# Bompa's Three Annual-Plan Cycle Types: Monocycle, Bicycle, Tricycle

**What it is** - Evans's slides (U3 L4 p.25-30, repeated identically in U3 L5 p.3-8), cited
throughout to "Bompa, 2009," present three annual-plan structures. Monocycle: "Only ONE
competition phase and one major peak," recommended "FOR NOVICE AND JUNIOR ATHLETES. LONG
PREPARATORY PHASE TO ENSURE DEVELOPMENT OF THE TECHNICAL/TACTICAL/PHYSICAL DOMAINS," with a
stated week distribution per 52-week cycle: Preparatory >= 32 weeks, Competitive 10-15 weeks,
Transition 5 weeks. Bicycle: "TWO competition phases and two major peaks," for "ADVANCED OR
ELITE ATHLETES WHO QUALIFY FOR NATIONAL CHAMPIONSHIPS. TRY TO KEEP THE PREPARATORY PHASES AS
LONG AS POSSIBLE TO ENSURE DEVELOPMENT," distribution per 26-week cycle: Preparatory 13 weeks,
Competitive 5-10 weeks, Transition 3 weeks. Tricycle: "THREE competition phases and three
major peaks," for "ADVANCED OR INTERNATIONAL-LEVEL ATHLETES. SOLID FOUNDATION IS INSTALLED AND
THEY CAN TOLERATE MULTIPLE PEAKS. 3 OR MORE," distribution per 17-18-week cycle: Preparatory
>= 8 weeks, Competitive 3-5 weeks, Transition 2-3 weeks. No book title beyond "Bompa" and the
year 2009 is given on the slides.

**Why it works** - The slides state the recommended athlete level and week distribution for
each cycle type but do not explain the physiological reasoning for why, for example, a
tricycle's shorter preparatory phase (>=8 weeks versus a monocycle's >=32) is appropriate only
for athletes who already have "a solid foundation... installed" - the mechanism (a trained
athlete needing less time to re-establish base qualities before specializing toward a peak) is
implied by the athlete-level guideline but not stated explicitly on these slides.

**When to apply** - As a first-pass structural choice when designing an annual plan: how many
distinct peaks does the competition calendar actually require, and does the athlete's training
age support the correspondingly shorter preparatory phases of a multi-cycle plan? Eric's
baseline's own annual-plan language treats the plan as "a flexible roadmap, not a fixed
contract," built around "the competition calendar, key non-training dates... and phase-by
-phase volume/intensity waves" (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.22-23`) without naming a specific monocycle/bicycle/
tricycle choice; this framework gives that flexible planning language a specific named
structural menu to choose from. For a sport like college football, with a single primary
competitive season, this framework's monocycle category (long preparatory phase, one major
peak window covering the season) is the closest fit among the three named here, though Evans
does not apply this specific framework to football in this lecture (his football example in
U3 L7-L8 proceeds directly to a 10-step build process without naming which of these three
cycle types it uses).

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - No book title, edition, or page number is given beyond
"Bompa, 2009," so these week-distribution figures cannot be verified against a primary source
within this ingest; the `periodization--bompa` book already staged in this library's vault
does not, based on its file listing reviewed for this ingest's dedup check, include an entry
titled around monocycle/bicycle/tricycle annual-plan types specifically (its files cover
LTAD, step loading, training effects, supercompensation, and general periodization
principles instead), so this is recorded as a distinct, not-yet-cross-checked secondary
citation. Do not apply these week counts rigidly to a sport whose season length does not match
the 52/26/17-18-week cycle lengths given (a college football season, for example, does not map
cleanly onto any of the three). Confidence is untested.

**Example** - No sport-specific worked example is given on these slides; the numbers are
presented as generic templates.

**Related** - [[framework--bompa-macrocycle-phase-objectives]] (the phase-by-phase objectives
within any of these three cycle types),
[[framework--ten-step-process-for-building-an-annual-plan]] (Evans's own applied process,
which does not explicitly name which of these three cycle types it uses). Reciprocal-link
suggestion: `periodization--bompa/_domain.md` or `_book.md` could note that this course
lecture cites a monocycle/bicycle/tricycle framework from the same author (Bompa, 2009) not
yet represented among that book's own staged entries, as a candidate for a future chapter
batch.

==> framework--bompa-macrocycle-phase-objectives.md <==

# Bompa's Macrocycle Phases and Their Stated Objectives: Preparatory, Competitive, Unloading/Tapering, Transition

**What it is** - Evans's slides (U3 L5 p.15-19), cited to "Bompa, 2009," list a macrocycle's
phases (Preparatory, split into General and Specific/Special; Competitive, split into
Pre-competitive and Main Competitive; Unloading/Tapering; Transition) with stated objectives
for each. Preparatory: "ACQUIRE AND IMPROVE GENERAL PHYSICAL TRAINING CAPACITY, IMPROVE THE
BIOMOTOR ABILITIES REQUIRED BY THE SPORT, CULTIVATE PSYCHOLOGICAL TRAITS, DEVELOP, IMPROVE,
PERFECT TECHNICAL ELEMENTS, FAMILIARIZE ATHLETES WITH THE BASIC STRATEGIC MANEUVERS MASTERED
IN THE FOLLOWING PHASES, TEACH ATHLETES THE THEORY AND METHODOLOGY OF TRAINING SPECIFIC TO THE
SPORT." Competitive: "CONTINUED IMPROVEMENT OR MAINTENANCE OF SPORT-SPECIFIC BIOMOTOR
ABILITIES, ENHANCING PSYCHOLOGICAL TRAITS, PERFECTING AND CONSOLIDATING TECHNIQUE, ELEVATING
PERFORMANCE TO THE HIGHEST LEVEL, DISSIPATING FATIGUE AND ELEVATING PREPAREDNESS, PERFECTING
TECHNICAL AND TACTICAL MANEUVERS, GAINING COMPETITIVE EXPERIENCE, MAINTAINING SPORT-SPECIFIC
FITNESS." Unloading/Tapering: "BEST WAY TO ELEVATE THE ATHLETE'S PREPAREDNESS AND STIMULATE A
SUPERCOMPENSATION OF PERFORMANCE THAT WILL INCREASE THE ATHLETE'S PERFORMANCE POTENTIAL DURING
THE COMPETITION," lasting "1-2 WEEKS." Transition: "FACILITATES PSYCHOLOGICAL REST,
RELAXATION, BIOLOGICAL REGENERATION, MAINTAINING AN ACCEPTABLE LEVEL OF GENERAL PHYSICAL
PREPARATION (40-50% OF COMPETITIVE PHASE)," associated with "DETRAINING."

**Why it works** - The slides state each phase's objectives as a list without explaining why
this specific ordering (general preparatory work before specific, tapering immediately before
competition, detraining-permissive transition after) produces better outcomes than an
alternative ordering; the underlying logic (build general capacity, narrow toward
sport-specificity, peak, then allow planned detraining before the next cycle) is implied by
the sequence itself but not argued for explicitly on these slides.

**When to apply** - As a template phase list when laying out any of the three annual-plan
cycle types from [[framework--bompa-annual-plan-cycle-types]]. Eric's baseline independently
documents a very similar general-to-specific sequence: "The preparatory period is sequenced
hypertrophy/work-capacity, then basic strength, then strength-to-power, each with defined
intensity/volume bands... before a transition into competition" (`method-baseline.md`,
"Periodization and programming," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.19-21`);
this Evans framework gives that baseline sequence a named phase-objective structure (General
Preparatory versus Specific Preparatory, Pre-competitive versus Main Competitive) that the
baseline material does not spell out at this level of detail.

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - As with the related cycle-types entry, no page or edition
is given beyond "Bompa, 2009," so this cannot be verified against a primary source within this
ingest, and the vault's `periodization--bompa` book does not, per its current file listing,
stage an entry matching this specific phase-objective breakdown. The Transition phase's "40-50%
of competitive phase" general-physical-preparation figure is stated without explaining what
baseline value that percentage is taken from (percentage of the competitive phase's volume?
intensity? Both are plausible readings and the slide does not disambiguate). Confidence is
untested.

**Example** - No sport-specific worked example is given on these slides.

**Related** - [[framework--bompa-annual-plan-cycle-types]],
[[framework--ten-step-process-for-building-an-annual-plan]] (Step Four of Evans's own later
process, "Setup Training Phases," names this same phase list directly).

==> framework--issurin-microcycle-types-and-planning-steps.md <==

# Issurin's Six Microcycle Types and a Six-Step Process for Planning Them

**What it is** - Evans's slide (U3 L5 p.21), cited to "Issurin, 2008," gives a table of six
microcycle types with Purpose, Load Level, and Duration (in days): Adjustment ("Initial
Adaptation To Appropriate Loads," Medium load, "Gradual Training Load Increase," 5-7 days);
Loading ("Fitness Development," Substantial-High load, "Use Of Big And Substantial
Workloads," 5-9 days); Impact ("Fitness Development Using Extreme Training Stimuli," Very
High-Extreme load, "Use And Summation Of Extreme Workloads," 4-7 days); Precomp ("Immediate
Preparation For Competition," Medium load, "Tuning For Comp, Using Event-Specific Means," 5-7
days); Comp ("Participation In Competition," High-Very High load, "Sport And Event-Specific
Performance," 2-7 days); Restoration ("Active Recovery," Low load, "Using Restorative Means,"
3-7 days). A separate slide (p.24), also cited to "Issurin, 2008," gives a six-step "Planning
Microcycles" process: (1) "Determination Of Dominant And Secondary Training Modalities," based
on the annual plan and current mesocycle's specificity; (2) "Determination, Placement And
Compilation Of Key Workouts," which "provide the main development impact of the training"; (3)
"Determination Of Restorative Workouts And Restorative 'Windows'," to "facilitate performance
of key-workouts and prevent excessive fatigue accumulation"; (4) "Determination, Placement And
Compilation Of Other Developmental And Supportive Workouts," noting "workload interaction
deserves special attention; preceding workouts affect sensitivity to subsequent workloads";
(5) "Selection Of Appropriate Means For Monitoring Training And For Follow-Up," targeted at
the abilities and functions the cycle addresses; (6) "Planning Special Events," which "can
involve a physician, dietitian, psychologist, special meetings, etc."

**Why it works** - The tables state each microcycle type's purpose, relative load, and typical
duration, and the six steps state a planning sequence, but neither slide explains the
physiological rationale for why, for example, an Impact microcycle's "extreme" loads should
be summed over 4-7 days specifically rather than a different duration; these are presented as
practitioner guidelines credited to Issurin, not derived from data shown on the slide.

**When to apply** - As a named vocabulary and sequencing checklist when building a microcycle
within a mesocycle: what type of microcycle is needed given the current training-stage goal,
and has the six-step process (dominant modality, key workouts, restorative windows, supportive
workouts, monitoring, special events) been followed in order? Evans's own later worked example
(U3 L7, Step Nine, "Setup Workouts within Microcycles") explicitly re-asks a subset of these
same questions ("What type of microcycle am I needing? Adjustment, Loading, Impact, etc.")
for a football wide receiver, showing this framework is meant to feed directly into his
10-step annual-plan process; see [[framework--ten-step-process-for-building-an-annual-plan]].
Eric's baseline does not name these six specific microcycle types, though its general
macro/meso/microcycle planning language (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and
programming") operates at the same structural level.

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - No page number is given beyond "Issurin, 2008," and this
book is separately staged in this library at `block-periodization--issurin`, whose own ingest
map (reviewed for this dedup check) shows Chapter 3, "Microcycles, mesocycles and training
stages" (printed pp.76-124), as the chapter that would contain this exact content, and that
chapter's status was "pending" (0 entries) as of this ingest. This entry should therefore be
treated as a preview of content the primary-source ingest has not yet atomized in full detail;
once `block-periodization--issurin` Chapter 3 is atomized, this entry should be checked against
it and corrected or merged if the primary source gives different duration ranges, load
descriptions, or step details than Evans's slide transcription. Confidence is untested.

**Example** - Evans's own football wide-receiver example (U3 L7-L8) applies this vocabulary
("What type of microcycle and I needing? Adjustment, Loading, Impact, etc.") without working
through a fully specified microcycle-by-microcycle plan in the material read for this ingest.

**Related** - [[framework--ten-step-process-for-building-an-annual-plan]]. Reciprocal-link
suggestion: `block-periodization--issurin/_book.md`'s recommended "Batch 2" (Chapter 3) should
cross-check this entry once atomized, since it covers "microcycle types (3.1)" per that
book's own chapter map.

==> framework--buzzichelli-integration-and-development-of-motor-capacities.md <==

# Buzzichelli's Integration and Development Models: Complex Versus Sequential Biomotor Training

**What it is** - Evans's slides (U3 L5 p.26-30), cited to "Buzzichelli, 2011," present a
"Periodization of Conditional Motor Capacities" framework with two named components relevant
to this entry. Integration: "the way motor capacity is trained in the annual plan; in
relation to the others," with two options: "Complex" ("Biomotor Abilities Are All Trained At
The Same Time") or "Sequential" ("Biomotor Abilities Are Emphasized At Different Times During
The Annual Plan"). Development: "the way each conditional motor capacity is trained during
the annual plan," with three named patterns: Complex development, illustrated at three
timescales - within a training unit ("MxS, Power, Muscular Endurance are trained within this
sequence within a single training session"), within a microcycle ("MxS, Power, ME are all
trained in the microcycle in different training workouts"), and within a mesocycle ("MxS,
Power, ME are trained throughout the mesocycle, during dedicated microcycles"); Sequential
development, distinguishing "Immediate Realization" ("At the end of the mesocycle, the
indexes of the trained biomotor quality are improved") from "Delayed Realization" ("At the
end of the mesocycle, the indexes... are depressed but improve later"); and Pendular
development ("Two qualities of biomotor abilities are trained in alternative fashion (e.g.,
Max Strength followed by Power followed by Max Strength followed by Power)"). No book title is
given beyond "Buzzichelli, 2011."

**Why it works** - The slides name the integration and development options and give brief
illustrative examples (MxS/Power/ME sequencing; the delayed-realization pattern) but do not
state the physiological mechanism for why a given quality shows delayed rather than immediate
realization, or how to predict in advance which pattern a given combination of qualities will
follow; this is presented as a descriptive taxonomy of observed or theorized patterns, not a
derived model.

**When to apply** - As vocabulary for describing how a program is choosing to combine
multiple biomotor qualities: are strength, power, and endurance work happening together
(complex) or in separate blocks (sequential), and within complex training, at what
timescale (session, microcycle, or mesocycle) is that combination happening? This connects
directly to Eric's baseline's training-compatibility constraint - incompatible qualities are
not trained together at full intensity, compatible ones are trained together, and the rest at
a retention dose (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.28-29`) - which is effectively a rule for choosing
between this framework's Complex and Sequential integration options based on quality
compatibility, though the baseline material does not use Buzzichelli's specific vocabulary.
The baseline's own delayed-transformation awareness (a 30-day residual-effect retraining
cadence for strength) is also consistent with, though not identical to, this framework's
"Delayed Realization" concept.

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - No page number or book title is given beyond "Buzzichelli,
2011," so this cannot be verified against a primary source within this ingest; this entry
should be treated as Evans's slide transcription of a secondary citation, not a confirmed
quotation. The slide gives no criteria for predicting, in advance, whether two given
qualities will show immediate or delayed realization when trained together - this can
apparently only be observed after the fact. Confidence is untested.

**Example** - The MxS/Power/Muscular-Endurance sequencing example given at the training-unit,
microcycle, and mesocycle timescales, described above, is the lecture's only worked
illustration, and it is generic (no specific sets, reps, or athlete given).

**Related** - [[framework--buzzichelli-load-progression-and-specificity-continuum]] (the
companion Load Progression and Specificity components of the same Buzzichelli, 2011
framework), [[principle--periodization-is-timing-not-time]].

==> framework--buzzichelli-load-progression-and-specificity-continuum.md <==

# Buzzichelli's Load Progression (Wave Loading) and Specificity Continuum (Complex Versus Sequential Training Means)

**What it is** - Continuing the same "Periodization of Conditional Motor Capacities"
framework cited to "Buzzichelli, 2011" (U3 L5 p.26, see also
[[framework--buzzichelli-integration-and-development-of-motor-capacities]]), two further
components are given. Load Progression (p.31-32): named "WAVE LOADING," applied at two
timescales - "Load within the mesocycle" and "Load within the microcycle" - with no further
elaboration or numeric example on these slides (bare diagram pages). Specificity of the
Training Means (p.33): a two-way distinction between "Complex" ("General And Specific
Training Means Are Utilized At The Same Time") and "Sequential" ("General Training Means
Precede Specific Training Means"). No book title is given beyond "Buzzichelli, 2011."

**Why it works** - The slide names "wave loading" at two timescales without stating a
mechanism for why a wave pattern (as opposed to, for example, a linear or step pattern; see
the vault's Bompa `framework--step-loading-paradigm.md` for a different named loading scheme)
is preferred at either the mesocycle or microcycle level, and without a numeric example of what
a wave actually looks like at either timescale. The Specificity distinction states that
general training means can either precede specific ones (Sequential) or run concurrently
(Complex), which mirrors the same general-to-specific structure found in Bondarchuk's
GPE/SPE/SDE/CE exercise-class continuum (already staged in this library at
`transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes.md`),
though Evans's slide does not explicitly connect the two.

**When to apply** - As a two-question check when programming a training block: is the load
progression across the mesocycle or microcycle following a deliberate wave pattern (rather
than, implicitly, a flat or purely linear one), and are general and specific training means
being run concurrently or in sequence? Eric's baseline's own preferred model, "undulating/

# Bompa's Three Annual-Plan Cycle Types: Monocycle, Bicycle, Tricycle

**What it is** - Evans's slides (U3 L4 p.25-30, repeated identically in U3 L5 p.3-8), cited
throughout to "Bompa, 2009," present three annual-plan structures. Monocycle: "Only ONE
competition phase and one major peak," recommended "FOR NOVICE AND JUNIOR ATHLETES. LONG
PREPARATORY PHASE TO ENSURE DEVELOPMENT OF THE TECHNICAL/TACTICAL/PHYSICAL DOMAINS," with a
stated week distribution per 52-week cycle: Preparatory >= 32 weeks, Competitive 10-15 weeks,
Transition 5 weeks. Bicycle: "TWO competition phases and two major peaks," for "ADVANCED OR
ELITE ATHLETES WHO QUALIFY FOR NATIONAL CHAMPIONSHIPS. TRY TO KEEP THE PREPARATORY PHASES AS
LONG AS POSSIBLE TO ENSURE DEVELOPMENT," distribution per 26-week cycle: Preparatory 13 weeks,
Competitive 5-10 weeks, Transition 3 weeks. Tricycle: "THREE competition phases and three
major peaks," for "ADVANCED OR INTERNATIONAL-LEVEL ATHLETES. SOLID FOUNDATION IS INSTALLED AND
THEY CAN TOLERATE MULTIPLE PEAKS. 3 OR MORE," distribution per 17-18-week cycle: Preparatory
>= 8 weeks, Competitive 3-5 weeks, Transition 2-3 weeks. No book title beyond "Bompa" and the
year 2009 is given on the slides.

**Why it works** - The slides state the recommended athlete level and week distribution for
each cycle type but do not explain the physiological reasoning for why, for example, a
tricycle's shorter preparatory phase (>=8 weeks versus a monocycle's >=32) is appropriate only
for athletes who already have "a solid foundation... installed" - the mechanism (a trained
athlete needing less time to re-establish base qualities before specializing toward a peak) is
implied by the athlete-level guideline but not stated explicitly on these slides.

# Bompa's Macrocycle Phases and Their Stated Objectives: Preparatory, Competitive, Unloading/Tapering, Transition

**What it is** - Evans's slides (U3 L5 p.15-19), cited to "Bompa, 2009," list a macrocycle's
phases (Preparatory, split into General and Specific/Special; Competitive, split into
Pre-competitive and Main Competitive; Unloading/Tapering; Transition) with stated objectives
for each. Preparatory: "ACQUIRE AND IMPROVE GENERAL PHYSICAL TRAINING CAPACITY, IMPROVE THE
BIOMOTOR ABILITIES REQUIRED BY THE SPORT, CULTIVATE PSYCHOLOGICAL TRAITS, DEVELOP, IMPROVE,
PERFECT TECHNICAL ELEMENTS, FAMILIARIZE ATHLETES WITH THE BASIC STRATEGIC MANEUVERS MASTERED
IN THE FOLLOWING PHASES, TEACH ATHLETES THE THEORY AND METHODOLOGY OF TRAINING SPECIFIC TO THE
SPORT." Competitive: "CONTINUED IMPROVEMENT OR MAINTENANCE OF SPORT-SPECIFIC BIOMOTOR
ABILITIES, ENHANCING PSYCHOLOGICAL TRAITS, PERFECTING AND CONSOLIDATING TECHNIQUE, ELEVATING
PERFORMANCE TO THE HIGHEST LEVEL, DISSIPATING FATIGUE AND ELEVATING PREPAREDNESS, PERFECTING
TECHNICAL AND TACTICAL MANEUVERS, GAINING COMPETITIVE EXPERIENCE, MAINTAINING SPORT-SPECIFIC
FITNESS." Unloading/Tapering: "BEST WAY TO ELEVATE THE ATHLETE'S PREPAREDNESS AND STIMULATE A
SUPERCOMPENSATION OF PERFORMANCE THAT WILL INCREASE THE ATHLETE'S PERFORMANCE POTENTIAL DURING
THE COMPETITION," lasting "1-2 WEEKS." Transition: "FACILITATES PSYCHOLOGICAL REST,
RELAXATION, BIOLOGICAL REGENERATION, MAINTAINING AN ACCEPTABLE LEVEL OF GENERAL PHYSICAL
PREPARATION (40-50% OF COMPETITIVE PHASE)," associated with "DETRAINING."

**Why it works** - The slides state each phase's objectives as a list without explaining why
this specific ordering (general preparatory work before specific, tapering immediately before
competition, detraining-permissive transition after) produces better outcomes than an
alternative ordering; the underlying logic (build general capacity, narrow toward
sport-specificity, peak, then allow planned detraining before the next cycle) is implied by
the sequence itself but not argued for explicitly on these slides.

**When to apply** - As a template phase list when laying out any of the three annual-plan
cycle types from [[framework--bompa-annual-plan-cycle-types]]. Eric's baseline independently
documents a very similar general-to-specific sequence: "The preparatory period is sequenced
hypertrophy/work-capacity, then basic strength, then strength-to-power, each with defined
intensity/volume bands... before a transition into competition" (`method-baseline.md`,
"Periodization and programming," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.19-21`);
this Evans framework gives that baseline sequence a named phase-objective structure (General
Preparatory versus Specific Preparatory, Pre-competitive versus Main Competitive) that the
baseline material does not spell out at this level of detail.

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - As with the related cycle-types entry, no page or edition
is given beyond "Bompa, 2009," so this cannot be verified against a primary source within this
ingest, and the vault's `periodization--bompa` book does not, per its current file listing,
stage an entry matching this specific phase-objective breakdown. The Transition phase's "40-50%
of competitive phase" general-physical-preparation figure is stated without explaining what
baseline value that percentage is taken from (percentage of the competitive phase's volume?
intensity? Both are plausible readings and the slide does not disambiguate). Confidence is
untested.

**Example** - No sport-specific worked example is given on these slides.

**Related** - [[framework--bompa-annual-plan-cycle-types]],
[[framework--ten-step-process-for-building-an-annual-plan]] (Step Four of Evans's own later
process, "Setup Training Phases," names this same phase list directly).

# Issurin's Six Microcycle Types and a Six-Step Process for Planning Them

**What it is** - Evans's slide (U3 L5 p.21), cited to "Issurin, 2008," gives a table of six
microcycle types with Purpose, Load Level, and Duration (in days): Adjustment ("Initial
Adaptation To Appropriate Loads," Medium load, "Gradual Training Load Increase," 5-7 days);
Loading ("Fitness Development," Substantial-High load, "Use Of Big And Substantial
Workloads," 5-9 days); Impact ("Fitness Development Using Extreme Training Stimuli," Very
High-Extreme load, "Use And Summation Of Extreme Workloads," 4-7 days); Precomp ("Immediate
Preparation For Competition," Medium load, "Tuning For Comp, Using Event-Specific Means," 5-7
days); Comp ("Participation In Competition," High-Very High load, "Sport And Event-Specific
Performance," 2-7 days); Restoration ("Active Recovery," Low load, "Using Restorative Means,"
3-7 days). A separate slide (p.24), also cited to "Issurin, 2008," gives a six-step "Planning
Microcycles" process: (1) "Determination Of Dominant And Secondary Training Modalities," based
on the annual plan and current mesocycle's specificity; (2) "Determination, Placement And
Compilation Of Key Workouts," which "provide the main development impact of the training"; (3)
"Determination Of Restorative Workouts And Restorative 'Windows'," to "facilitate performance
of key-workouts and prevent excessive fatigue accumulation"; (4) "Determination, Placement And
Compilation Of Other Developmental And Supportive Workouts," noting "workload interaction
deserves special attention; preceding workouts affect sensitivity to subsequent workloads";
(5) "Selection Of Appropriate Means For Monitoring Training And For Follow-Up," targeted at
the abilities and functions the cycle addresses; (6) "Planning Special Events," which "can
involve a physician, dietitian, psychologist, special meetings, etc."

**Why it works** - The tables state each microcycle type's purpose, relative load, and typical
duration, and the six steps state a planning sequence, but neither slide explains the
physiological rationale for why, for example, an Impact microcycle's "extreme" loads should
be summed over 4-7 days specifically rather than a different duration; these are presented as
practitioner guidelines credited to Issurin, not derived from data shown on the slide.

**When to apply** - As a named vocabulary and sequencing checklist when building a microcycle
within a mesocycle: what type of microcycle is needed given the current training-stage goal,
and has the six-step process (dominant modality, key workouts, restorative windows, supportive
workouts, monitoring, special events) been followed in order? Evans's own later worked example
(U3 L7, Step Nine, "Setup Workouts within Microcycles") explicitly re-asks a subset of these
same questions ("What type of microcycle am I needing? Adjustment, Loading, Impact, etc.")
for a football wide receiver, showing this framework is meant to feed directly into his
10-step annual-plan process; see [[framework--ten-step-process-for-building-an-annual-plan]].
Eric's baseline does not name these six specific microcycle types, though its general
macro/meso/microcycle planning language (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and
programming") operates at the same structural level.

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - No page number is given beyond "Issurin, 2008," and this
book is separately staged in this library at `block-periodization--issurin`, whose own ingest
map (reviewed for this dedup check) shows Chapter 3, "Microcycles, mesocycles and training
stages" (printed pp.76-124), as the chapter that would contain this exact content, and that
chapter's status was "pending" (0 entries) as of this ingest. This entry should therefore be
treated as a preview of content the primary-source ingest has not yet atomized in full detail;
once `block-periodization--issurin` Chapter 3 is atomized, this entry should be checked against
it and corrected or merged if the primary source gives different duration ranges, load
descriptions, or step details than Evans's slide transcription. Confidence is untested.

**Example** - Evans's own football wide-receiver example (U3 L7-L8) applies this vocabulary
("What type of microcycle and I needing? Adjustment, Loading, Impact, etc.") without working
through a fully specified microcycle-by-microcycle plan in the material read for this ingest.

**Related** - [[framework--ten-step-process-for-building-an-annual-plan]]. Reciprocal-link

# Buzzichelli's Integration and Development Models: Complex Versus Sequential Biomotor Training

**What it is** - Evans's slides (U3 L5 p.26-30), cited to "Buzzichelli, 2011," present a
"Periodization of Conditional Motor Capacities" framework with two named components relevant
to this entry. Integration: "the way motor capacity is trained in the annual plan; in
relation to the others," with two options: "Complex" ("Biomotor Abilities Are All Trained At
The Same Time") or "Sequential" ("Biomotor Abilities Are Emphasized At Different Times During
The Annual Plan"). Development: "the way each conditional motor capacity is trained during
the annual plan," with three named patterns: Complex development, illustrated at three
timescales - within a training unit ("MxS, Power, Muscular Endurance are trained within this
sequence within a single training session"), within a microcycle ("MxS, Power, ME are all
trained in the microcycle in different training workouts"), and within a mesocycle ("MxS,
Power, ME are trained throughout the mesocycle, during dedicated microcycles"); Sequential
development, distinguishing "Immediate Realization" ("At the end of the mesocycle, the
indexes of the trained biomotor quality are improved") from "Delayed Realization" ("At the
end of the mesocycle, the indexes... are depressed but improve later"); and Pendular
development ("Two qualities of biomotor abilities are trained in alternative fashion (e.g.,
Max Strength followed by Power followed by Max Strength followed by Power)"). No book title is
given beyond "Buzzichelli, 2011."

**Why it works** - The slides name the integration and development options and give brief
illustrative examples (MxS/Power/ME sequencing; the delayed-realization pattern) but do not
state the physiological mechanism for why a given quality shows delayed rather than immediate
realization, or how to predict in advance which pattern a given combination of qualities will
follow; this is presented as a descriptive taxonomy of observed or theorized patterns, not a
derived model.

**When to apply** - As vocabulary for describing how a program is choosing to combine
multiple biomotor qualities: are strength, power, and endurance work happening together
(complex) or in separate blocks (sequential), and within complex training, at what
timescale (session, microcycle, or mesocycle) is that combination happening? This connects
directly to Eric's baseline's training-compatibility constraint - incompatible qualities are
not trained together at full intensity, compatible ones are trained together, and the rest at
a retention dose (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.28-29`) - which is effectively a rule for choosing
between this framework's Complex and Sequential integration options based on quality
compatibility, though the baseline material does not use Buzzichelli's specific vocabulary.
The baseline's own delayed-transformation awareness (a 30-day residual-effect retraining
cadence for strength) is also consistent with, though not identical to, this framework's
"Delayed Realization" concept.

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - No page number or book title is given beyond "Buzzichelli,
2011," so this cannot be verified against a primary source within this ingest; this entry
should be treated as Evans's slide transcription of a secondary citation, not a confirmed
quotation. The slide gives no criteria for predicting, in advance, whether two given
qualities will show immediate or delayed realization when trained together - this can
apparently only be observed after the fact. Confidence is untested.

**Example** - The MxS/Power/Muscular-Endurance sequencing example given at the training-unit,
microcycle, and mesocycle timescales, described above, is the lecture's only worked
illustration, and it is generic (no specific sets, reps, or athlete given).

**Related** - [[framework--buzzichelli-load-progression-and-specificity-continuum]] (the
companion Load Progression and Specificity components of the same Buzzichelli, 2011
framework), [[principle--periodization-is-timing-not-time]].

==> claim--body-composition-is-a-prediction-not-a-measurement.md <==

# "Body Composition Analysis Is NOT a Measurement, It Is a Prediction"

**What it is** - Evans states directly (U3 L6 p.6, slide titled "Body Composition Reality"):
"Body composition analysis is NOT a measurement, it is a PREDICTION. Want to get a true
measurement of body fat? Carcass Analysis... so you're telling me I have to be dead to get my
body fat measured?" (paraphrased rhetorical framing, quoted as close to the slide's own
phrasing as its sparse text allows). The following slides (p.7-9) list body-composition models
(Two, Three, and Four Compartment) and the most widely used field methods (Hydrostatic
Weighing, BodPod, DEXA, Bioelectrical Impedance, Skinfolds), with a table of stated error
rates: for small/population-level error versus large/individual-level error, respectively -
Underwater Weighing 0.1-2.1% versus 5%+, BodPod 2% versus 6%+, Bioelectrical Impedance 8-9%
(no separate individual-level figure given), Skinfolds 6% versus 10-15% (with a further note,
"Tracking over time... different?" and a second Skinfolds figure of 3-5%, not reconciled with
the first on this slide), DEXA 1-2% versus 4-10%.

**Why it works** - Evans's own reasoning is that only carcass analysis (necessarily
post-mortem) directly measures body fat, so every practical field method is instead a
statistical prediction from indirect proxies (impedance, X-ray absorption, skinfold
thickness, water displacement); this is a stated epistemic point about measurement validity,
not a physiological mechanism claim. Inference: the practical implication is that
population-level error rates (the more favorable numbers in the table) should not be
mistaken for individual-athlete accuracy, since the same slide explicitly separates
population from individual error and reports individual-level error as substantially higher
for every method shown.

**When to apply** - As a caution when reporting or discussing body-composition numbers with
coaches or athletes: treat any single body-fat percentage as an estimate with a real
error margin, not a precise fact, and prefer within-method, within-device tracking over time
(the slide's own unreconciled second Skinfolds figure, 3-5% for "tracking over time," hints at
this without stating it clearly) over comparing absolute numbers across different measurement
methods. Eric's baseline notes DEXA and body-composition assessment as owned by Performance
Nutrition, not Applied Performance, with body-composition testing capped at four times per
year (`method-baseline.md`, "Nutrition and body composition," citing
`ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md`), which is consistent with treating body-composition
testing as a lower-frequency, imprecise-instrument measure rather than a high-frequency
precise one.

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - The slide's own Skinfolds error figures are internally
inconsistent (6% and 10-15% on one line, 3-5% on the next, with no stated reconciliation
between "error rate" and "tracking over time" framings); both are recorded here rather than
silently resolved. No citation year or source is given for the compiled error-rate table
itself, so its provenance cannot be verified from this lecture. Confidence is untested.

**Example** - The error-rate table itself, described above, is the lecture's worked
illustration; no specific athlete case is given.

**Related** - None found elsewhere in this library specifically comparing body-composition
method error rates at population versus individual level (checked by grep for "DEXA" and
"body composition" combined with "error rate").

==> framework--sport-specific-test-battery-model.md <==

# Build the Testing Battery Around a Test-Order Protocol and Sport-Specific Rationale, Not a Generic Checklist

**What it is** - Evans's slides (U3 L6) give two related pieces. First, "Assessment
Considerations" (p.3): Athlete Preparation (diet, training, testing), Test Environment
(surface, cleanliness, temperature, time of day), Test Order ("Non Physical -> Physical (High
Velocity -> Low Velocity)"), and an Equipment Checklist & Assignments (per drill/activity:
equipment required, test procedures, who is in charge of testing and data collection). Second,
three worked sport-specific battery tables, each with a Test and a stated Rationale column
(p.20-22): for Track Cyclists in a velodrome - Anthropometry (assess body composition), VO2Max
("Cyclists on Track are often characterized with high aerobic power"), Alactic Peak Power, 6s
("Examine the alactic power mechanism specific in the leg musculature"), 30-min Time Trial
("'Race of Truth'. No tactics involved (drafting)"), Movement Screen; for Basketball -
Anthropometry (assess and compare against positional values), Vertical Jump ("common feature
in offensive and defensive movements"), Sprints 5/10/20m (acceleration and speed), Right/Left
Shuffle Line-to-Line Drill (anaerobic-glycolytic capacity), Yo-Yo Intermittent Test (aerobic
capacity), 1-6RM Squat/Bench (maximal contractile qualities), Movement Screen; for Rowers -
Anthropometry, a 7x4-min Incremental Test based on best 2000m time (submaximal capacity,
efficiency, and training zones from lactate and HR data), 1-6RM Squat/Bench Pull/Clean
(maximal strength qualities), Movement Screen.

**Why it works** - The test-order rule (non-physical before physical, high-velocity before
low-velocity) is stated without an explicit mechanism on this slide, though the general logic
in sport-science practice (not stated by Evans here) is that fatigue from a low-velocity or
high-fatigue test can degrade performance on a subsequent high-velocity test if the order is
reversed; this is Inference, not something the slide itself explains. The three sport-battery
tables each pair a test to a stated rationale tied to that sport's specific demands (aerobic
power for track cycling's sustained efforts, vertical jump for basketball's offensive/
defensive movements, a 2000m-based incremental test for rowing's specific event distance),
demonstrating the general principle that test selection should follow from event-specific
demands rather than a single universal battery.

**When to apply** - As a template for building any sport's testing battery: state the
rationale for each test in terms of that sport's specific demands, and sequence tests
non-physical-to-physical and high-velocity-to-low-velocity within a session. Eric's baseline
independently documents an equivalent sport-specific battery approach at Baylor: "The Baylor
Sport Assessment Table (V4) assigns a specific battery per sport (movement screen,
anthropometrics, CMJ, broad jump, weighted throw, upper/lower strength estimation, strength
endurance, aerobic fitness, repeat sprint ability, linear sprint, change of direction) rather
than testing every sport the same way" (`method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment," citing
`update-baylor-sport-assessment-table-v4.md`) - the same underlying principle (sport-specific
battery, not one-size-fits-all) that Evans's three worked examples illustrate, though neither
source's specific test list matches the other's exactly (Baylor's V4 table is not reproduced
in Eric's baseline in enough detail to compare test-by-test against Evans's track-cyclist,
basketball, and rower examples).

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - These three battery examples are for track cycling,
basketball, and rowing specifically; none is football, so none can be directly copied for a
Baylor football application without independent sport-specific reasoning. The test-order
rationale (non-physical before physical, high-velocity before low-velocity) is stated as a
rule without a cited source or exception cases (e.g., whether a movement screen, arguably
"non-physical" in intensity but requiring some physical performance, fits cleanly into this
binary). Confidence is untested.

**Example** - The three sport-battery tables (track cyclist, basketball, rower) described
above are the lecture's worked examples.

**Related** - [[framework--ten-step-process-for-building-an-annual-plan]] (Step Ten of that
process, "Setup Assessment & Monitoring," names testing frequency without this level of
sport-specific rationale detail). No existing entry in the vault or staging library matches
Evans's specific track-cyclist, basketball, or rower battery tables (checked by grep).

==> framework--ten-step-process-for-building-an-annual-plan.md <==

# Evans's Ten-Step Process for Building an Annual Plan (American Football Wide Receiver Example)

**What it is** - Evans presents a ten-step sequence for building an annual plan (U3 L7),
applied throughout to "Sport: American Football, Position: Wide Receiver" (p.2). Step One,
"Build Profile": a table of System, Notes, and Rationale covering Autonomic NS
(parasympathetic dominance, for "fast recovery abilities, resiliency"), Central NS (high
central drive, for "speed of movement, reaction time, tactical decision making"),
Neuromuscular (large fast-twitch percentage especially lower body, large concentric/eccentric
loading, for "speed of movement, deceleration qualities"), Energy Supply Systems (per
time-motion analysis: alactic and aerobic capacity), Common Injuries (ankle, knee, hip,
shoulder, fingers, informing "exercise prescription, loading strategies"), and
Anthropometrics (low body fat percent, moderate cross-sectional area for force production and
collisions). Step Two: "Setup Calendar" (competitions, travel, intensive practice periods,
organizational dates, holidays, training camps/facilities). Step Three: "Setup Periodization
Model" (single/double/triple periodization, team-sport considerations). Step Four: "Setup
Training Phases" (Preparatory-General/Specific, Competition-Precompetitive/Main, Unloading/
Tapering, Transition - see [[framework--bompa-macrocycle-phase-objectives]]). Step Five:
"Setup Bioenergetic Sequence" (per athlete profile/TMA; aerobic, anaerobic-glycolytic,
anaerobic-alactic; power vs. capacity, time to develop, developmental potential). Step Six:
"Setup Biodynamic Sequence" (per profile, periodization model, phases, bioenergetics;
exercises classified GPE/SPE/SDE/Competitive - a classification already staged in this
library's primary-source Bondarchuk entries, not re-atomized here). Step Seven: "Setup
Biomotor Sequence" (strength, speed, endurance, flexibility/mobility, skill; e.g. "Maximal
-strength SPE vs SDE," "Alactic capacity SPE vs SDE"). Step Eight: "Setup Mesocycles and
Microcycles" (calendar-driven duration; loading strategies - Step, Wave, Flat; mesocycle
dominant themes - Primary/Secondary/Tertiary; Complex vs. Sequential sequencing; days per
week; facilities). Step Nine: "Setup Workouts within Microcycles" (mesocycle theme; microcycle
type per [[framework--issurin-microcycle-types-and-planning-steps]]; key-workout placement;
supplemental workouts). Step Ten: "Setup Assessment & Monitoring" (assessments; monitoring
frequency - Daily, X per Week, Biweekly, Monthly, Quarterly, Yearly). The lecture closes with
a single unelaborated slide, "SLEEP ON IT" (p.13).

**Why it works** - Evans does not state why this specific ten-step order (profile before
calendar, calendar before periodization model, bioenergetics before biodynamics before
biomotor) is necessary rather than some other sequence; Inference: the order appears designed
so that each step's output becomes an input constraint for the next (the athlete's profile and
the competition calendar constrain which periodization model and phases are feasible, which in
turn constrain the bioenergetic, biodynamic, and biomotor sequencing choices, which in turn
determine mesocycle and microcycle and workout design, with assessment and monitoring set up
last to track the resulting plan) - but Evans does not argue for this dependency structure
explicitly in the lecture; it is read from the sequence itself.

**When to apply** - As a step-by-step checklist when building any annual plan from scratch, for
football or another sport, ensuring the athlete profile and calendar constraints are
established before periodization, phase, and sequencing decisions are made. Eric's baseline
does not document an equivalent explicit ten-step process; its closest parallel is the
department's own three-phase Playbook Development Plan roadmap (Foundation, Operational
Depth, Education and Culture, `method-baseline.md`, "Department model and roles"), which
operates at the departmental-documentation level rather than the individual-athlete
annual-plan level this framework addresses. This framework's Step One profile table (ANS,
CNS, neuromuscular, energy systems, injuries, anthropometrics) is a more granular
starting-point checklist than anything named in the baseline's testing and assessment
material.

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - This entire ten-step sequence is applied only to a
hypothetical, illustrative "American Football, Wide Receiver" profile, not to a named real
athlete; the Step One profile values (parasympathetic dominance, large fast-twitch
percentage, low body fat) are stated as generic assumptions about "a wide receiver" as a
position archetype, not as measured data from any specific player. Do not treat this as a
validated planning method; it demonstrates Evans's own applied teaching sequence, and no
outcome data (whether a plan built this way produced better results than an alternative
sequence) is given anywhere in this lecture. Confidence is untested. The Step Six exercise
classification (GPE/SPE/SDE/CE) is not re-atomized as its own entry here because it
duplicates primary-source content already staged at
`transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes.md`.

**Example** - The entire lecture is the worked example: a football wide receiver's Step One
profile, described above, carried through all ten steps. The continuation into a specific
weekly loading template appears in the next lecture; see
[[case-study--wide-receiver-preparatory-phase-weekly-loading-template]].

**Related** - [[framework--bompa-annual-plan-cycle-types]],
[[framework--bompa-macrocycle-phase-objectives]],
[[framework--issurin-microcycle-types-and-planning-steps]],
[[case-study--wide-receiver-preparatory-phase-weekly-loading-template]].

# Worked Example: A Wide Receiver's Preparatory-Phase Weekly Loading Template

**What it is** - Continuing the hypothetical "American Football, Wide Receiver" annual-plan
example from U3 L7 (see
[[framework--ten-step-process-for-building-an-annual-plan]]), Evans gives a specific weekly
structure for two preparatory sub-phases. Preparatory I, General (p.3-4, 11-12): duration 4-5
weeks, training days Monday/Tuesday/Thursday/Friday, 8 hours per week ("CARA" - Countable
Athletically Related Activities), indoor turf and weight room available at all times; loading
by day - Sunday/Wednesday/Saturday off (Small), Monday Medium, Tuesday Substantial-Large,
Thursday Medium, Friday Substantial-Large; session focus - Monday/Thursday "Aerobic Capacity /
UB Focus" (extensive runs, upper body weights, extensive medicine-ball throws, torso work),
Tuesday/Friday "Alactic Power / LB Focus" (sprints, jumps, intensive medicine-ball throws,
lower body weights). Preparatory I, Specific (p.13-16): duration 3-4 weeks, same weekly
structure and facilities, loading by day - Sunday/Wednesday/Saturday off (Small), Monday
Medium, Tuesday "Substantial-Large/Extreme," Thursday Medium, Friday Substantial-Large;
session focus unchanged (Monday/Thursday Aerobic Capacity/UB with "Extensive Runs/Drills"
replacing plain "Extensive Runs," Tuesday/Friday Alactic Power/LB with "Sprints/Drills"
replacing plain "Sprints").

**Why it works** - Evans does not explain why this specific day-of-week loading pattern
(Tuesday and Friday as the two highest-load days, bracketing a Medium Monday and Thursday,
with three low/off days) was chosen over an alternative arrangement, nor why the General
sub-phase's 4-5 weeks shortens to 3-4 weeks in the Specific sub-phase; Inference: the
alactic-power/lower-body Tuesday-Friday pairing and aerobic-capacity/upper-body
Monday-Thursday pairing appears designed to separate the two energy-system emphases named in
the Step Five bioenergetic sequence (alactic and aerobic, see
[[framework--ten-step-process-for-building-an-annual-plan]]) onto different training days
rather than combining them in the same session, consistent with the general
training-compatibility logic in [[principle--periodization-is-timing-not-time]], but this
specific rationale is not stated by Evans in this lecture.

**When to apply** - As a concrete template for how a general-to-specific preparatory
progression can be laid out week-to-week for a skill-position football athlete, separating
aerobic-capacity/upper-body work from alactic-power/lower-body work by day. Eric's baseline
does not include a comparably detailed weekly loading template for any specific position; the
Exam 3 Study Guide's own item 62 ("Alactic power speed distance comparison between offensive
lineman vs wide receiver") and item 64-65 (SPE/SDE lower-body exercise choices for a wide
receiver) confirm that Evans intended this position-specific comparison (lineman vs. wide
receiver) as a further teaching point, but the specific comparative numbers were not found on
the slide pages read for this ingest (they appear to be discussed verbally, not shown in the
slide text).

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - This is an illustrative teaching template for a
hypothetical wide receiver, not data from any real athlete, team, or season; no actual
performance outcomes, injury data, or adherence data are given anywhere in this lecture to
support that this specific loading pattern is effective. The "8 hours per week (CARA)" and
NCAA-specific facility-availability framing tie this template to US college athletics
countable-hours rules, which Evans references elsewhere in the course as a real constraint
("NCAA reality? CARA hours..." U3 L3 p.12, p.16) but does not re-explain in this lecture; a
reader unfamiliar with NCAA countable-athletically-related-activity rules should not assume
this 8-hour figure applies outside that specific regulatory context. Confidence is untested.

**Example** - The weekly template itself, described above, is the example.

**Related** - [[framework--ten-step-process-for-building-an-annual-plan]],
[[principle--periodization-is-timing-not-time]].

==> framework--adime-monitoring-process.md <==

# ADIME: Assessment, Diagnosis, Intervention, Monitoring and Evaluation

**What it is** - Evans's slide (U4 L1 p.12) names a four-step "step process" labeled ADIME:
Step 1, Assessment; Step 2, Diagnosis; Step 3, Intervention; Step 4, Monitoring & Evaluation,
shown as a cycle. No citation or source discipline is named for this specific acronym on the
slide (ADIME is a model with origins in clinical dietetics/nutrition-care process
terminology, but Evans does not state this origin in this lecture, so that connection is
Inference, not something the slide says). The lecture also gives a monitoring definition,
credited by name: "'A set of activities designed to help establish the acute training status
of an athlete, so that appropriate and timely training adjustments can take place to ensure
ongoing performance targets are attained.' - Dave Hamilton, Great Britain Women's Hockey S&C
Coach" (p.13).

**Why it works** - The slide presents ADIME as a cyclical process without stating why these
four specific steps, in this order, are necessary; Inference: the cyclical arrow shown on the
slide (Monitoring & Evaluation feeding back toward Assessment) implies that the process is
meant to repeat, with each cycle's monitoring data informing the next cycle's assessment,
though this feedback loop is not explicitly narrated by Evans in this lecture.

**When to apply** - As a named four-step structure for organizing a monitoring program:
assess current status, diagnose what needs to change, intervene (design the training
response), then monitor and evaluate the result before the cycle repeats. Evans's own later
"Summary" lecture (U4 L3 p.11) repeats this exact four-step diagram without additional
elaboration, confirming it as one of the course's core recurring frameworks. Eric's baseline
does not name ADIME specifically, though its own testing philosophy (assessment is
continuous, informing ongoing training adjustment, `method-baseline.md`, "Testing and
assessment") shares the same underlying assess-then-adjust logic without this specific
four-step vocabulary or the "Diagnosis" step named explicitly.

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - No book, paper, or original context is cited for the
ADIME acronym itself in this lecture (only the year-less "Dave Hamilton" quote is separately
attributed for the monitoring definition, not for ADIME); do not assume ADIME originates with
Hamilton, since the slide does not make that connection explicitly. This is a compressed
process label, not a validated monitoring protocol with specific test choices; it must be
filled in with the actual assessment and intervention content from elsewhere in this lecture
(see [[framework--monitoring-toolkit-by-domain-frequency-cost]]) to be operationally useful.
Confidence is untested.

**Example** - No specific worked example applying all four ADIME steps to one athlete is
given in this lecture.

**Related** - [[framework--monitoring-toolkit-by-domain-frequency-cost]],
[[heuristic--monitoring-is-a-compass-not-a-gps]].

==> framework--monitoring-toolkit-by-domain-frequency-cost.md <==

# A Monitoring Toolkit Organized by Domain, with Named Tools, Frequency, and Relative Cost

**What it is** - Evans's slides (U4 L1 p.16-19) organize monitoring tools into four domains,
each with named solutions, a suggested frequency, and (for three of the four) a relative cost
tier ($ = Low/None, $$ = Moderate, $$$ = High). Nutrition/Body Composition: Bodyweight
(weekly), Skinfolds (biweekly or monthly), Body Comp Analyzers - DEXA, Hydrostatic, InBody,
BodPod (no more than 4x per year), Blood Biomarkers via a sports medicine hospital or LabCorp
(3-4x per year, "focus on simple biomarkers, e.g. serum ferritin, D3"), with a stated minimum
of "Performance metrics + Body Composition." Psychological: Profile of Mood States (monthly,
$), Recovery-Stress Questionnaire for Athletes (weekly, $), Daily Analysis of Life Demands for
Athletes (weekly, $), Smith Relaxation States Inventory (weekly, $), sRPE "used to calculate
training load, monotony, strain" (daily, $), a custom soreness/sickness/lethargy questionnaire
(daily-weekly, $) - all marked for team-sport use with checkmarks or "Best Athletes" only.
Movement/Muscle: FMS, PCA, isolated muscle testing (e.g. groin squeeze), isolated joint ROM
(e.g. total arc) - "Full screen during critical times, individual tests more frequently," no
cost tier given. Physical Fitness: Jump Tests (Bosco, DJ-RSI, SJ, CMJ, "ES or 2x," $), Sprint
Tests 10-20yds (1x, $), Weight Exercises via Linear Transducers (1-2x, $$-$$$), Player
Tracking/GPS ("Every field based session," $$$), Aerobic Tests via Heart Rate Recovery (1x,
$-$$), Training Load (sRPE x Duration, "Best athletes," ES, $), Monotony (Average Daily
Training Load / Standard Deviation of Weekly Training Load, "Best athletes," ES, $), Strain
(Monotony x Weekly Training Load, "Best athletes," ES, $), Heart Rate Variability ("Best
Athletes," ED, $-$$$). ("ES" and "ED" are used on the slide without a stated legend; Inference:
likely "Every Session" and "Every Day" respectively, given the monitoring-schedule table on
the following page (p.22) uses "ED" for HRV and "ES" for RPE and Bosco jump testing, both of
which are typically administered daily or every session.)

**Why it works** - The slides state which tools exist and at what frequency and cost, but do
not explain why each specific frequency was chosen (e.g., why skinfolds biweekly-or-monthly
rather than weekly) beyond the general "start simple and small, be very consistent" philosophy
stated on the closing slide (see [[heuristic--monitoring-is-a-compass-not-a-gps]]).

**When to apply** - As a menu for building a monitoring program within resource constraints,
by choosing tools across the four domains that fit a program's budget (using the cost tiers as
a guide) and testing capacity (using the frequency guidance and the "Best Athletes"-only
option for more expensive or time-consuming tools). Eric's baseline documents a broadly
consistent multi-domain approach at Baylor (force-plate CMJ testing, GPS/Catapult load
monitoring, SmartSpeed timing, VALD suite tools, `method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and
neuromuscular monitoring," "Load monitoring and GPS," "Speed and sprint"), and this Evans
framework's cost-tiering and "Best Athletes only" triage concept is not explicitly named in
the baseline material reviewed, though the baseline's own decision to retire roster-wide
NordBord testing in favor of targeted use for "smaller numbers, clear clinical purpose,
dedicated oversight" (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring," citing
`2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md`) reflects the same underlying triage logic this
framework's "Best Athletes" column encodes for other tools.

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - The "ES" and "ED" abbreviations are not defined on the
slide itself; the reading given above is Inference from context (the monitoring-schedule table
on the following page), not a stated definition, and should be verified against the CVASPS
transcript or another source before being treated as certain. No cost tier is given for the
Movement/Muscle domain tools. The Monotony and Strain formulas are given without a worked
numeric example or citation to the original sports-science literature (these formulas
originate with Foster's training-monotony/strain model, but Evans's slide does not name Foster
or any other source). Confidence is untested.

**Example** - No single-athlete worked example combining tools across all four domains is
given in this lecture; the monitoring-schedule table (p.22) shows a 12-week schedule template
with HRV (ED), RPE (ES), Bosco jump testing (2x), Bodyweight (1x), Body Fat % (occasional
checkmarks), and POMS/QUEST (occasional/ES) but does not name a specific athlete.

**Related** - [[framework--adime-monitoring-process]],
[[heuristic--monitoring-is-a-compass-not-a-gps]],
[[claim--big-data-monitoring-without-training-theory-is-noise]].

==> heuristic--monitoring-is-a-compass-not-a-gps.md <==

# "Monitoring Is a Compass, Not a GPS Unit"

**What it is** - Evans's closing slide (U4 L1 p.23, "closing thoughts") states, in his own
words: "Monitoring is a compass, not a GPS unit. Only utilize it if you believe in the
literature and will utilize it to make adjustments to the training process. Start simple and
small, but be very consistent. Sometimes the cheaper options provide better insight. Don't get
offended if the data is showing your training plan is not working as well as you think it
should. LEARNING MOMENT!"

**Why it works** - This is a stated coaching philosophy about how to interpret monitoring
data, not a mechanism claim; Evans does not explain what makes monitoring "a compass" (general
directional guidance) rather than "a GPS unit" (precise positional data) beyond the framing
itself. Inference: the practical implication is that monitoring data should inform the
general direction of a training adjustment (are we trending toward fatigue, toward
readiness) rather than being trusted as a precise, standalone answer for exactly what to do
next - consistent with his own earlier conclusion that no single overtraining biomarker is a
definitive diagnostic (see [[claim--no-definitive-diagnostic-tool-for-overtraining-syndrome]]).

**When to apply** - As a framing reminder when introducing a monitoring program to staff or
athletes: expect directional trends, not precise answers, and be prepared to revise the
training plan when the data disagrees with it, treating that disagreement as useful
information rather than a threat. This is directly consistent with Eric's baseline's own
stated data-collection discipline: "Data collection has a cost in time, athlete compliance,
and staff attention. When the insight stops justifying that cost, it's time to stop
collecting" (`method-baseline.md`, "Philosophy and decision principles," citing
`2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md`), and with the baseline's own account of retiring
subjective wellness surveys and roster-wide NordBord testing when they stopped producing
trustworthy, actionable signal (`method-baseline.md`, "Load monitoring and GPS," "Force plate
and neuromuscular monitoring") - both share this heuristic's premise that monitoring's value
is instrumental (does it change what you do) rather than automatic.

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - This is a general philosophy statement, not a specific
decision rule; it does not say which specific metrics function well as "compass"-type
directional signals versus which might mislead. "Start simple and small" and "sometimes the
cheaper options provide better insight" are stated as Evans's own recommendations without a
supporting citation or specific example of a cheap option outperforming an expensive one.
Confidence is untested.

**Example** - No specific worked example (a named metric or athlete case) is given on this
slide.

**Related** - [[claim--no-definitive-diagnostic-tool-for-overtraining-syndrome]],
[[framework--adime-monitoring-process]].

==> claim--big-data-monitoring-without-training-theory-is-noise.md <==

# Carl Valle's Critique, as Quoted by Evans: Monitoring Without Training-Theory Comprehension Is "Ornamental Data" and "a Suicide Mission"

**What it is** - Evans's slide (U4 L2 p.5) quotes Carl Valle directly: "Monitoring instead of
creating insight to the responses of athletes to training, is now creating a data and
information dark age in regards to the understanding of training, by poorly appreciating the
basic principles." And: "Without fully comprehending the training process, monitoring is
nothing more than observational recordings of a suicide mission, resulting in ornamental data
displayed real time for coaches to find a purpose because they are too fearful to train." No
publication or year is given for the quote beyond the name "Carl Valle." The surrounding
slides name a five-step "ACQUIRE, MANAGE, ANALYZE, VISUALIZE, ACTION" pipeline (p.6) and list
"Practical Reasons to Monitor" as Athlete Feedback, Coach Feedback, and Medical Team/Return to
Play (p.8), both without further elaborating text on the pages read for this ingest (pages 9-20
are bare diagram pages with no extractable text).

**Why it works** - This is a quoted critique from a named source (Carl Valle, previously
listed among Evans's "my influences" in U4 L1 p.2), not a claim Evans states in his own voice
in this slide; its argument, as quoted, is that monitoring technology can substitute for
(rather than support) genuine understanding of training theory, producing data that looks
authoritative ("ornamental data displayed real time") without actually informing coaching
decisions, driven by coaches' fear of committing to a training decision without a data
justification.

**When to apply** - As a caution against adopting monitoring technology as a substitute for
training-theory competence, particularly relevant given how much of this course (Units 1-3)
is devoted to training theory before Unit 4 introduces monitoring tools - a sequencing that
itself may reflect this same Carl Valle premise (theory before monitoring). Eric's baseline
shares a structurally similar caution in a different context: the Nordbord retirement
decision was explicitly framed around whether a program has "smaller numbers, clear clinical
purpose, dedicated oversight" to make a test's data meaningful, not simply whether the test is
valid or affordable (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring," citing
`2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md`) - both sources share the premise that data
collection without the capacity or understanding to act on it correctly is of limited or
negative value.

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - No publication, year, or context is given for this Carl
Valle quote in the lecture; it cannot be verified against a primary source within this ingest.
The "ACQUIRE, MANAGE, ANALYZE, VISUALIZE, ACTION" pipeline named on the following slide is not
elaborated with any specific content in the pages read (pages 7-20 are largely bare diagrams
without extractable text), so it is mentioned here only as a label, per the rule that a slide
naming a concept without elaboration should say so, not treated as its own separate framework
entry. Confidence is untested.

**Example** - No specific athlete or program example is given in this lecture; the quote is
presented as a general critique.

**Related** - [[framework--monitoring-toolkit-by-domain-frequency-cost]],
[[heuristic--monitoring-is-a-compass-not-a-gps]],
[[claim--no-definitive-diagnostic-tool-for-overtraining-syndrome]].

==> claim--weight-room-transfer-limited-without-dynamic-correspondence.md <==

# Weight-Room Exercises Provide "Little Insight" on Field Performance When They Fail Dynamic-Correspondence Criteria

**What it is** - Evans states directly (U4 L1 p.5): "Most Important: Special Work Capacity...
Movement & Energetic potential relative to the sporting demands. Primary Questions (Needs
Analysis): What are the movements required? Dynamic Correspondence. What are the dominant
energy systems fueling those movements? Weight room exercises? Provide little insight on how
they will perform on their respective field of play. Why? Minimal DC criteria met." He then
immediately qualifies this, anticipating pushback (p.5): "Whoa there. You saying the weight
room is not important? Absolutely not!"

**Why it works** - Evans's own stated reasoning is that weight-room exercises typically meet
only some of the Dynamic Correspondence criteria (see
[[case-study--dynamic-correspondence-applied-to-wrestling-takedown]] for the five-factor
checklist) relative to a given sport's actual competitive movements, so a weight-room test
result (e.g., a back squat max) does not directly indicate how that capacity will express
itself in the sport-specific movement pattern; he does not, in this slide, specify which of the
five Dynamic Correspondence criteria weight-room exercises typically fail, only that "minimal
DC criteria" are met in general.

**When to apply** - As a caution against treating weight-room testing (1RM lifts, jump tests
performed in isolation from the sport skill) as a direct proxy for on-field performance,
without denying that weight-room training itself contributes to Special Work Capacity. This
connects directly to a broader theme in Eric's baseline: "A test can be scientifically valid
and still be the wrong choice operationally... even a valid test stops being valuable" without
the infrastructure and interpretation context to use it well (`method-baseline.md`,
"Philosophy and decision principles," citing `2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md`).
Evans's claim here is a related but distinct point: not about operational sustainability of a
test, but about a testing method's inherent limits in predicting a different outcome (field
performance) than the one it directly measures (weight-room capacity).

**When NOT to apply - mandatory** - Evans does not name which specific weight-room exercises
he has in mind, nor does he give an example of measuring "how well" a given weight-room result
predicted (or failed to predict) actual field performance for any real athlete; this is a
conceptual claim, not a data-backed one, in this lecture. He also does not specify a threshold
for "minimal DC criteria met" versus a higher, more sport-corresponding threshold that would
change this conclusion. Confidence is untested. Do not read this claim as recommending against
weight-room training generally; Evans explicitly disclaims that reading in the same breath he
makes the claim.

**Example** - No specific exercise-to-sport-skill comparison is worked through in this
lecture; the wrestling takedown analysis from U2 L4 (see
[[case-study--dynamic-correspondence-applied-to-wrestling-takedown]]) is the course's only
detailed worked Dynamic Correspondence example, applied to a competitive skill rather than to
a weight-room exercise directly.

**Related** - [[framework--two-factors-special-work-capacity-technical-mastery]],
[[case-study--dynamic-correspondence-applied-to-wrestling-takedown]].

(daily-weekly, $) - all marked for team-sport use with checkmarks or "Best Athletes" only.
Movement/Muscle: FMS, PCA, isolated muscle testing (e.g. groin squeeze), isolated joint ROM
(e.g. total arc) - "Full screen during critical times, individual tests more frequently," no
cost tier given. Physical Fitness: Jump Tests (Bosco, DJ-RSI, SJ, CMJ, "ES or 2x," $), Sprint
Tests 10-20yds (1x, $), Weight Exercises via Linear Transducers (1-2x, $$-$$$), Player
Tracking/GPS ("Every field based session," $$$), Aerobic Tests via Heart Rate Recovery (1x,
$-$$), Training Load (sRPE x Duration, "Best athletes," ES, $), Monotony (Average Daily
Training Load / Standard Deviation of Weekly Training Load, "Best athletes," ES, $), Strain
(Monotony x Weekly Training Load, "Best athletes," ES, $), Heart Rate Variability ("Best
Athletes," ED, $-$$$). ("ES" and "ED" are used on the slide without a stated legend; Inference:
likely "Every Session" and "Every Day" respectively, given the monitoring-schedule table on
the following page (p.22) uses "ED" for HRV and "ES" for RPE and Bosco jump testing, both of
which are typically administered daily or every session.)

not explain why each specific frequency was chosen (e.g., why skinfolds biweekly-or-monthly
rather than weekly) beyond the general "start simple and small, be very consistent" philosophy
stated on the closing slide (see [[heuristic--monitoring-is-a-compass-not-a-gps]]).

**When to apply** - As a menu for building a monitoring program within resource constraints,
by choosing tools across the four domains that fit a program's budget (using the cost tiers as
a guide) and testing capacity (using the frequency guidance and the "Best Athletes"-only
option for more expensive or time-consuming tools). Eric's baseline documents a broadly
consistent multi-domain approach at Baylor (force-plate CMJ testing, GPS/Catapult load

framework's cost-tiering and "Best Athletes only" triage concept is not explicitly named in
the baseline material reviewed, though the baseline's own decision to retire roster-wide
